E-Commerce Customer Intelligence Report

Project Description¶

The Business Problem¶

A UK-based online gift store has 13 months of raw transaction data sitting in a spreadsheet. Management knows their total revenue but has no visibility into who their best customers are, why customers are not coming back, or where revenue is silently leaking out. Without this information, every marketing and retention decision is a guess.

What This Analysis Does¶

This report applies a full four-layer analytical framework to 541,909 real transactions — moving from surface-level observations to root cause diagnosis to mathematical revenue projections:

Phase Question Answered
Descriptive What is actually happening in this business?
Diagnostic Why is it happening?
Prescriptive What should the business do about it?
Predictive (CLV Model) What is each customer worth going forward?

Dataset¶

  • Source: UCI Machine Learning Repository — Online Retail Dataset
  • Period: December 2010 — December 2011
  • Size: 541,909 raw transactions lines· 4,335 unique customers · 38 countries
  • Revenue: £10,642,110 total across 13 months

Tools Used¶

Python · Pandas · NumPy · Matplotlib · Seaborn · Jupyter Notebook

Executive Summary

Analyst: CJ John Paulin  |  Date: 2026  |  Dataset: UCI Online Retail — 541,909 real transactions · Dec 2010 – Dec 2011

What This Report Covers¶

This report analyzes 13 months of real transaction data from a UK-based online gift store — covering 4,335 customers, 524,878 transactions after removing cancellations/returns for revenue calculations, and £10,642,110 in total revenue. It identifies three urgent business problems the store's standard reports are not showing, and provides specific actions with projected financial impact.

⚠ Problem 1 — £893,980 Is Silently Leaking Out Every Year¶

The store lost £893,980 to cancellations — 7.7% of gross revenue — across 3,836 cancellation invoices. This number does not appear in standard sales dashboards. The store's top quantity product, PAPER CRAFT, LITTLE BIRDIE, is simultaneously its most cancelled product at £168,470 in lost revenue — suggesting a fulfillment or quality issue that is costing the business on both ends.

Additionally, 34.4% of customers bought only once and never returned. Every marketing pound spent acquiring these customers generated zero repeat value.

Fix: Investigate the top cancelled product immediately. Set up a post-purchase email within 7 days of first purchase to convert one-time buyers into repeat customers.

⚠ Problem 2 — The Entire Business Depends on 434 People¶

RFM analysis reveals that 1,315 Champion customers generate 72.97% of all revenue — and the top 10% of customers (just 434 people) account for 61.4% of annual revenue (£5,367,688). The business does not know who these people are or have any formal system to keep them.

Cohort analysis confirms the retention crisis — 78.2% of new customers never return after their first purchase. Month 1 retention sits at just 21.8%, meaning nearly 8 in 10 new customers are acquired and immediately lost.

Meanwhile, 765 At Risk customers representing £929,327 in revenue are quietly drifting away — still reachable but going silent.

Fix: Identify Champions by name using the RFM list in this report. Launch a VIP loyalty program this month. Send a win-back campaign to At Risk customers within 30 days before they become Lost.

✅ Opportunity — £2,107,329 in Recoverable Revenue¶

Acting on the recommendations in this report — three targeted email campaigns over 90 days — is projected to recover £2,107,329 in additional annual revenue under the Realistic scenario:

Action What Changes Revenue Recovered
Post-purchase email sequence Retention 21.8% → 30% £1,518,196
At Risk win-back campaign 20% of 765 customers return £185,866
Loyal upsell bundles 100 customers move to Champion spend £403,267
Total £2,107,329

The Customer Lifetime Value model confirms a Champion is worth £4,367 per year — making a £50 VIP reward a 8,634% return on investment.

Three Actions for Monday Morning¶

1. Export the Champion customer list from the RFM analysis and send a personal thank-you email this week. These 1,315 customers generate £6,380,162 annually — they deserve to know they are valued.

2. Set up one automated email triggered 7 days after a customer's first purchase. Even moving Month 1 retention from 21.8% to 30% recovers £1,518,196 per year — automatically, every month, with no ongoing effort.

3. Send a time-limited win-back offer to the 765 At Risk customers this month. A 15% discount costs roughly £85 per customer recovered against a CLV of £425 — a 400% return on the campaign spend.

Bottom Line¶

The store is generating £10.6M in annual revenue while silently losing £893,980 to cancellations, £929,327 to drifting At Risk customers, and an estimated £2,107,329 to poor retention — a combined £3,931,229 in preventable annual revenue loss that three email campaigns and one loyalty program could significantly reduce.

Full methodology, data cleaning audit, and supporting analysis available in sections D1–P3 of this report.

D1 Insights — Monthly Revenue Trend¶

What the data shows¶

Revenue fluctuated across the first three quarters of 2011 with no consistent upward trend, before surging sharply in Q4 (Sep–Nov 2011). The business shows a clear seasonal concentration pattern rather than steady growth.

Key Findings¶

  • Peak month: November 2011 at £1,503,866 — nearly 3x the worst performing month
  • Worst month: February 2011 at £522,545 — the deepest revenue trough in the dataset
  • Q4 surge (Sep–Nov) drove disproportionate annual revenue, consistent with holiday gift-buying behavior for a gift store
  • Total annual revenue: £10,642,110 across 13 months of trading
  • Average order value remained stable at £18–25 throughout the year — revenue swings were driven by order volume, not spending per order

This means...¶

The business is heavily seasonal and volatile — Q4 carries a disproportionate share of annual revenue while February represents a significant cash flow risk. A store this dependent on Q4 demand needs either a mid-year promotional strategy to smooth revenue gaps or lean inventory planning for slow months to protect margins.

D2 Insights — Product Performance¶

What the data shows¶

The top revenue products and top quantity products are largely different lists — confirming that volume does not equal profitability in this store. High-quantity products tend to be low unit price items while high-revenue products command premium pricing.

Key Findings¶

  • Top revenue product: "REGENCY CAKESTAND 3 TIER" generating £174,156.54 in total sales
  • Top quantity product: "PAPER CRAFT , LITTLE BIRDIE" with 80,995 units sold
  • 6 products appear in both top 10 lists — these are the store's core products driving both volume and revenue simultaneously
  • Products in the revenue list but not the quantity list are high-margin premium items — fewer sales, higher value per sale

This means...¶

The store has two distinct product tiers — volume drivers and revenue drivers. A client managing this store should protect inventory for products appearing in both lists first, since losing stock on those items simultaneously hurts both revenue and order volume.

D3 Insights — Geographic Revenue Analysis¶

What the data shows¶

The store is overwhelmingly UK-dependent — the United Kingdom accounts for approximately 84.6% of total revenue. International markets collectively contribute a small but meaningful share, led by European countries dominating the top international markets list.

Key Findings¶

  • United Kingdom: £9,001,744.09 — 84.6% of total revenue
  • Top international market: Netherlands at £285,446.34
  • European dominance: 8 of the top 10 international markets are European, reflecting the store's geographic proximity advantage
  • EIRE and Netherlands show wholesale buyer patterns — EIRE generates £283,140 from only 3 customers (£94,380 avg per customer) while Germany generates £228,678 from 94 customers (£2,433 avg). This 39x difference in revenue per customer suggests EIRE and Netherlands are bulk wholesale accounts, not retail consumers

This means...¶

The store's heavy UK concentration is both a strength and a risk — stable domestic demand but significant vulnerability if UK consumer sentiment shifts. International expansion requires two distinct strategies — a wholesale partnership approach for markets like EIRE and Netherlands where bulk buyers already exist, and a retail marketing approach for Germany and France where broad consumer demand is present but underdeveloped.

D4 — Cancellation Analysis

Objective: Quantify the revenue impact of cancellations and identify which months, countries, and products are most affected.

Key metric: Revenue lost = absolute value of (Quantity × UnitPrice)
Why this matters: Cancellations represent real lost revenue that rarely appears in standard sales reports — making this one of the most actionable findings for a store owner.

D4 Insights — Order Cancellations¶

What We Found¶

Over the 13-month period, the business lost £893,980 from cancelled orders.

This represents 7.7% of total revenue, meaning that for every £13 earned, about £1 was later lost through cancellations.

Because cancelled orders are often hidden within sales reports, this is one of the biggest opportunities to recover lost revenue.

Key Findings¶

  • Total revenue lost to cancellations: £893,980
  • Cancellation rate: 7.7%
  • Cancelled invoices: 3,836 orders
  • Highest cancellation month: December 2011 (£205,089)
    • This was also the highest sales month, showing that cancellations increase as order volume increases.
  • Most cancelled product: PAPER CRAFT, LITTLE BIRDIE
    • Revenue lost from cancellations: £168,470
    • This product was also the store's best-selling item by quantity, which may indicate product quality, stock, or fulfillment issues.
  • Most cancellations came from the United Kingdom
    • Total cancelled revenue: £812,492
    • This is expected since the UK generates most of the store's sales.
  • Discount-related transactions appear among the most cancelled items.
    • This suggests some cancelled orders may be linked to promotions or discounts that were later reversed.

Business Impact¶

A 7.7% cancellation rate is a significant revenue leak.

Reducing cancellations by just 1 percentage point could recover approximately £89,000 in annual revenue.

The biggest opportunity appears to be PAPER CRAFT, LITTLE BIRDIE, which is both a top-selling and top-cancelled product. Investigating why customers cancel this item could help recover a substantial portion of the £168,470 currently being lost.

Recommended Actions¶

  1. Review the cancellation reasons for PAPER CRAFT, LITTLE BIRDIE.
  2. Check for stock availability, fulfillment delays, or quality issues.
  3. Analyze discount-related cancellations separately to identify avoidable reversals.
  4. Monitor cancellations during peak sales periods, especially around the holiday season.
  5. Set a target to reduce the cancellation rate from 7.7% to below 7%, which could generate meaningful additional revenue.

D5 Insights — Customer Purchase Behavior¶

What the data shows¶

The store has 4,338 unique customers (4,335 after removing records with missing CustomerID, used in all subsequent analysis) but purchase behavior is heavily right-skewed — the majority of customers buy only once while a small group of high-frequency buyers places a disproportionate share of all orders. The mean orders per customer (4.27) significantly exceeds the median (2 orders per customers), confirming this skew.

"Note: 3 CustomerIDs were later excluded from RFM/CLV analysis due to missing values, resulting in 4,335 customers in subsequent sections."

Key Findings¶

  • 34.4% of customers bought only once — the largest single customer segment represents a significant churn risk since they have never returned after their first purchase
  • 65.6% are repeat buyers — these customers are the store's most valuable asset and the primary target for retention investment
  • Top customer placed 209 orders — an extreme outlier likely representing a wholesale account consistent with the D3 finding on EIRE and Netherlands
  • Mean (4.27) vs Median (2) gap confirms a small number of high-frequency buyers are pulling the average up — most customers purchase far less frequently than the mean suggests

This means...¶

The store's customer base follows a classic power law distribution — a small number of high-value repeat buyers drive a disproportionate share of revenue while the majority are one-time purchasers who never return. This makes RFM segmentation essential — without identifying and protecting the high-frequency segment, the store risks losing its most valuable customers without even knowing who they are.

Phase 2 — Diagnostic Analysis —Why it Happened?

G1 — RFM Analysis — Customer Segmentation

Objective: Score every customer on Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value to identify which customers are Champions, Loyal, At Risk, Lost, or inactive.

Technique: RFM Scoring — each customer receives a score of 1–4 on each dimension. Combined scores determine their segment.

Dimension Definition High Score Means
Recency (R) Days since last purchase Bought recently
Frequency (F) Number of unique orders Buys often
Monetary (M) Total revenue generated Spends more

Why this matters: Without RFM, every customer looks the same. With RFM, the business knows exactly who to retain, who to reactivate, and who to let go.

G1 Insights¶

What the data shows¶

RFM scoring reveals that the store's 4,335 customers are not equal — they fall into distinct behavioral segments with dramatically different revenue contributions. A small group of Champions generates a disproportionate share of total revenue while a combined 1,079 Lost customers represent recoverable revenue if reactivated.

Segment Breakdown¶

  • Champions (1,315 customers) — bought recently (avg 17 days ago), buy often (9.34 orders avg), and spend the most (£4,851 avg). They drive 72.97% of total revenue despite representing only 30.3% of the customer base. These are the store's most critical asset — losing even 10% of Champions would erase approximately £638,000 in annual revenue.

  • At Risk (765 customers) — previously active buyers whose recency has slipped to 84 days on average. They still have reasonable frequency (3.27 orders) and spend (£1,214 avg) but are drifting. They represent £929,327 in revenue at risk — the highest recoverable amount of any non-Champion segment.

  • Loyal (608 customers) — recent buyers (23 days avg) with moderate frequency. Second most recent segment after Champions. Prime candidates for upselling — they are engaged but spending significantly less than Champions (£819 vs £4,851 avg).

  • Lost — Was Loyal (563 customers) — formerly frequent buyers now silent for 234 days on average. They have purchase history and brand familiarity making them more recoverable than pure Lost customers. A win-back campaign targeting this segment could recover a portion of the £440,538 they previously spent.

  • Lost (516 customers) — absent for 263 days with only 1 average order. Lowest recovery probability — minimal retention investment recommended here.

  • New Customers (259 customers) — recent first-time buyers (27 days avg) who have not yet returned. The critical window to convert them to Loyal or Champion status is now — engagement in the first 30 days after purchase significantly increases repeat purchase probability.

The Most Critical Finding¶

72.97% of revenue comes from 30.3% of customers — the Champions.
This is more concentrated than the classic 80/20 rule — it is effectively a 73/30 concentration. The business is one competitor campaign away from a catastrophic revenue drop if Champions are not actively retained.

This means...¶

The store has a three-priority retention strategy hiding in this data. First — protect Champions through exclusive loyalty rewards and early access programs before competitors target them. Second — reactivate At Risk customers immediately since their £929,327 at-risk revenue is still recoverable within a 30-day window. Third — convert New Customers within 30 days through targeted follow-up campaigns before the 34.4% one-time buyer pattern from D5 claims another cohort.

G2 Insights — Cohort Retention Analysis¶

What the data shows¶

Cohort analysis tracks what percentage of customers who first purchased in a given month returned in subsequent months. The retention heatmap reveals a consistent and steep drop between Month 0 and Month 1 across every cohort — confirming that the first 30 days after acquisition is the most critical and most at-risk retention window in this business.

Key Findings¶

  • Month 1 retention averages 21.8% — meaning 78.2% of new customers never return after their first purchase. This directly explains the 34.4% one-time buyer rate identified in D5 and represents the single largest recoverable revenue opportunity in the dataset
  • Retention stabilizes at approximately 22-25% after Month 3 — customers who survive the critical first 3 months demonstrate significantly more consistent long-term purchase behavior, suggesting a loyalty threshold exists at the 90-day mark
  • December 2010 cohort is the strongest — 885 customers acquired, maintaining 35-40% retention across most months and peaking at 50.2% in Month 11. This cohort likely contains the majority of current Champion segment customers identified in G1
  • December 2011 cohort has only 41 new customers — the sharp drop in acquisition reflects the dataset ending mid-December, not a real business decline
  • Largest acquisition month was December 2010 (885 customers) — consistent with the Q4 seasonal surge identified in D1, confirming that holiday season drives both revenue and new customer acquisition simultaneously

The Critical Retention Window¶

The average retention curve shows a near-vertical drop from 100% to 21.8% between Month 0 and Month 1 — then relative stability from Month 1 onward. This pattern has a specific business implication: the battle for customer loyalty is won or lost in the first 30 days. Customers who return once are likely to keep returningustomers who do not return in Month 1 almost never come back.

This means...¶

The store is losing 78% of new customers within 30 days of their first purchase with no apparent retention mechanism in place. A post-purchase email sequence triggered within 7 days of first purchase — offering a personalized product recommendation or a time-limited second-purchase discount — could meaningfully move the Month 1 retention rate. Even improving Month 1 retention from 21.8% to 30% across the average cohort size of 318 customers would retain approximately 26 additional customers per month — compounding into significant lifetime value as those customers move toward the Champion segment.

G3 Insights — Revenue Concentration Analysis¶

What the data shows¶

The store's revenue is heavily concentrated in a small group of customers. A tiny fraction of buyers is responsible for the vast majority of income — meaning the business is far more dependent on repeat high-value customers than it probably realizes.

Key Findings¶

  • Top 26.1% of customers generate 80% of revenue — slightly less concentrated than the classic 80/20 rule, but still means 8 out of 10 pounds comes from roughly 1 in 4 customers
  • Top 10% of customers generate £5,367,688 (61.4% of revenue) — just 434 customers are responsible for more than half of all money the store makes
  • Top 20% of customers generate £6,523,813 (74.6% of revenue) — 868 customers out of 4,335 carry three quarters of the entire business
  • Champions segment alone generates 73.0% of revenue (£6,380,162) — this one group is worth more than all other customer segments combined
  • At Risk segment has £929,327 drifting away — these 765 customers used to buy regularly but are now going quiet. They have not left yet — but they are heading that way

The Business Risk in Plain English¶

If the store lost its top 10% of customers tomorrow — just 434 people — it would lose £5,367,688 or 61.4% of annual revenue. No marketing campaign can replace that quickly. At the store's current rate of acquiring and retaining new customers, rebuilding that revenue would take years.

This means...¶

The store is essentially running on the loyalty of a small group of high-value customers without knowing it. If those customers leave, the business is in serious trouble. The smart move is to identify these customers by name using the RFM Champion list, treat them differently from everyone else, and make them feel valued before a competitor does. At the same time, the 765 At Risk customers represent £929,327 that is still recoverable — reaching out to them now, before they fully disengage, is the single highest return action the store can take today.

Prescriptive — What should the business do?

P1 — Customer Retention Strategy

The Core Recommendation¶

Not all customers deserve the same attention. Based on the RFM analysis, the store should follow a three-priority strategy — protect the customers keeping the business alive, recover the ones drifting away, and stop wasting money on customers who will never return.

Segment 1 — Champions

**1,315 customers · 73.0% of revenue · Avg spend £4,851**

These customers are the business. Losing even 10% of them means losing £638,016 in annual revenue — more than the entire At Risk, Loyal, and Lost segments combined.

What to do:

  • Create a VIP loyalty program — reward points on every purchase redeemable for discounts. Champions already buy frequently (avg 9.34 orders) so points accumulate fast, giving them a reason to stay
  • Send a personal thank-you — a simple email acknowledging their loyalty and offering an exclusive early access to new products costs nothing and builds emotional connection
  • Survey them — ask what products they want that the store does not carry yet. Champions spending £4,851 on average know exactly what they want. Their answers are free market research
  • Never let them go quiet — if a Champion has not purchased in 30 days, trigger an automatic check-in email with a personalized product recommendation based on their purchase history

Why this matters: Champions buy every 17 days on average. A 30-day silence is an early warning signal — not a normal gap.

Segment 2 — At Risk

**765 customers · £929,327 at risk · Last purchase avg 84 days ago**

These customers used to buy regularly. They have not left yet but they are going quiet. The window to recover them is now — every week of delay makes recovery harder.

What to do:

  • Launch a win-back campaign this month — send a targeted email with the subject line "We miss you" and a 10-15% discount on their most frequently purchased product category
  • Focus on Q4 — your data shows revenue per £1 spent doubles in Q4. At Risk customers who responded to offers before are most likely to respond again during the holiday season
  • Set a 30-day deadline — At Risk customers who do not respond to a reactivation offer within 30 days should be moved to the Lost segment and deprioritized. Do not keep spending on non-responders

Why this matters: £929,327 is still recoverable. Even reactivating 20% of At Risk customers recovers approximately £185,865 — enough to fund a full year of retention campaigns.

Segment 3 — Loyal

**608 customers · £498,047 revenue · Last purchase avg 23 days ago**

Loyal customers are buying recently and consistently but spending significantly less than Champions (£819 vs £4,851 avg). They are the most natural candidates to become Champions with the right push.

What to do:

  • Upsell with bundle offers — if a Loyal customer regularly buys product A, offer them a bundle of A + B at a small discount. Increasing their average order value moves them closer to Champion monetary scores
  • Offer a spending milestone reward — "Spend £1,000 this month and unlock VIP status." Give them a visible target to reach
  • Do not discount heavily — Loyal customers are already buying without incentive. Deep discounts train them to wait for sales rather than buying at full price

Why this matters: Converting even 100 Loyal customers to Champions at the Champion average spend of £4,851 adds approximately £403,200 in incremental annual revenue.

Segment 4 — Lost — Was Loyal

**563 customers · £440,538 historical revenue · Silent for avg 234 days**

These customers were once regular buyers but have been gone for nearly 8 months on average. They are harder to recover than At Risk but still worth one serious attempt given their historical spend.

What to do:

  • Send one win-back email with a strong offer — a 20-25% discount or a free gift with purchase. Make it time-limited (7 days) to create urgency
  • If they do not respond — stop — do not send multiple follow-up emails. Customers gone for 234 days who ignore one strong offer are unlikely to respond to weaker ones. Respect their decision and redirect that budget elsewhere
  • Track who responds — any Lost — Was Loyal customer who reactivates should be immediately moved into the At Risk nurture sequence to prevent them going quiet again

Why this matters: A 15% reactivation rate on this segment recovers approximately 84 customers with an expected £782 average spend — adding roughly £65,688 in recovered revenue.

Segment 5 — Lost and Needs Attention

**825 customers combined · £405,151 revenue · Minimal recovery probability**

Lost customers (516) have only placed 1 order on average and have been silent for 263 days. Needs Attention (309) are similarly inactive. Both segments have the lowest RFM scores across all three dimensions.

What to do:

  • Do not invest in retention campaigns for this group — the cost of reaching 825 customers with offers that have low probability of response is better spent protecting Champions and reactivating At Risk
  • Send one low-cost reactivation email — a simple "Here is what is new at our store" newsletter with no discount. If they click, add them to the At Risk nurture sequence. If they do not, remove them from active marketing lists
  • Use their data differently — analyze what these customers bought and when they left. If a pattern emerges (e.g. they all bought the same product category and never returned) that is a product quality signal worth investigating

Why this matters: Every pound spent trying to recover Lost customers is a pound not spent protecting Champions. Prioritization is the strategy.

Priority Summary¶

Priority Segment Action Revenue Impact
🔴 1st Champions VIP program + survey + 30-day alert Protect £6,380,162
🔴 2nd At Risk Win-back campaign this month Recover £185,865 (20%)
🟡 3rd Loyal Upsell bundles + milestone rewards Add £403,200 potential
🟡 4th Lost — Was Loyal One strong offer, 7-day deadline Recover £65,688 (15%)
🟢 5th Lost + Needs Attention One newsletter, then deprioritize Minimal spend

This means...¶

The store does not need a bigger marketing budget — it needs a smarter one. The data shows exactly who to spend on, in what order, and with what message. Focusing 80% of retention budget on Champions and At Risk customers while spending minimally on Lost segments is the highest return allocation the business can make with the information available today.

P2 — Revenue Recovery Projection

Objective: Quantify the financial impact of acting on the P1 retention recommendations using three scenarios — Pessimistic, Realistic, and Optimistic.

Model inputs sourced from:

  • G2 — Month 1 retention rate (21.8%) and avg cohort size (318)
  • G1 — At Risk segment size (765) and avg spend (£1,214)
  • G1 — Loyal segment size (608) and Champion avg spend (£4,851)

Key assumption: Projections assume average spend per customer remains consistent with observed RFM values. Results are directional estimates, not guaranteed outcomes. Actual results depend on campaign execution quality and market conditions.

Retention target:         25%
Additional customers/yr:  122

Stream 3 — Conversion:    £201,633.50

=== Realistic Scenario ===
Description:              Moderate effort — structured campaigns

Stream 2 — Reactivation:  £185,865.93
Stream 3 — Conversion:    £403,267.00
TOTAL RECOVERY:           £2,107,328.76

=== Optimistic Scenario ===

Stream 3 — Conversion:    £806,534.00
TOTAL RECOVERY:           £4,501,453.53

What this model shows¶

Using real customer data from the RFM and cohort analysis, this model projects how much additional annual revenue the store can recover by acting on three simple retention initiatives — keeping new customers, winning back drifting ones, and encouraging moderate spenders to buy more.

Three Scenarios — Pick Your Level of Effort¶

Scenario What It Takes Extra Revenue Per Year
🟠 Pessimistic One automated email after first purchase £887,033
🔵 Realistic Three targeted campaigns over 3 months £2,107,329
🟢 Optimistic Full VIP program + all campaigns £4,501,454

Where the Money Comes From¶

Each scenario pulls from three revenue streams:

Stream What Changes Realistic Recovery
1 — Keep new customers longer Retention improves 21.8% → 30% £1,518,196
2 — Win back At Risk customers 20% of 765 customers return £185,866
3 — Move Loyal to Champion spend 100 customers spend more £403,267

The Minimum Action Worth Taking¶

Even the Pessimistic scenario — a single automated post-purchase email requiring one afternoon of setup — recovers £887,033 per year. That email runs automatically every month with zero ongoing effort.

Assumptions¶

  • Customer average spend stays consistent with current values
  • Campaign quality is competent — poor execution lowers results
  • These are directional estimates, not guaranteed outcomes

This means...¶

The store is leaving at least £887,000 on the table every year with no retention system in place. The Realistic scenario recovers £2,107,329 through three email campaigns — a few hours of work that pays for itself many times over.

P3-Customer Lifetime Value Model

Objective: Calculate how much each RFM customer segment is worth to the business over the next 12 months — giving the store a clear number to put against any retention investment.

Formula used:

CLV = Average Order Value × Annual Purchase Frequency × Retention Rate

Why this matters: Knowing a Champion is worth £X per year makes the cost of a loyalty program — say £50 per customer — an obvious investment, not a guessed expense.

What is CLV?¶
Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) is simply how much money
the store can expect from one customer over the next 12 months
based on how they currently buy. It answers the question every
store owner should ask before spending on marketing:




"Is this customer worth spending money on — and how much?"

Max to spend = 20% of CLV — the safe limit to stay profitable

What This Means in Plain English¶
    

  • A Champion customer is worth £4,367 to the business
over the next year. Spending £50 on a VIP reward for them
returns £4,317 — a no-brainer investment.
    

    • 

  • An At Risk customer is worth £425 if reactivated.
A 15% discount offer costs roughly £60 per customer.
If even half respond, the campaign pays for itself
many times over.
    

    • 

  • A Lost customer is worth only £25. One email is
justified. Anything more wastes budget that should
go toward Champions and At Risk.
    

    • 





Total Portfolio Value¶
The store's 4,335 existing customers are worth a combined
£6,547,599 over the next 12 months — assuming current
buying behavior continues unchanged.


Acting on the P1 and P2 recommendations grows this number.
Doing nothing shrinks it as At Risk customers drift to Lost.




This means...¶
The store now has a number for every customer type.
No more guessing whether a discount or loyalty reward
is worth it — compare the cost to the CLV and the
answer is always clear. Protect the £4,367 Champions
first. Recover the £425 At Risk customers second.
Stop spending on the £25 Lost customers entirely.
